title: Migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base with your coding agent
abstract: With a customer-managed knowledge base on Amazon Bedrock , you provision and scale the vector store, tune the embedding model and index settings, and plan capacity for each new data source. The migration guide in the Agent Toolkit for AWS helps you migrate to Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base . Managed Knowledge Base takes over that work and adds new retrieval capabilities, and your team keeps control of the content and the application that uses it. Moving a production knowledge base means your team maps its configuration, creates the replacement, ingests content, updates the application’s retrieval call, and validates retrieval before switching traffic. To help, we added a knowledge base migration guide to the amazon-bedrock skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS . The guide gives your coding agent the context to plan the migration with you, starting with read-only discovery and a plan you review line by line. On your approval, the agent creates the new knowledge base and its data sources alongside the original, or writes a migrated infrastructure as code (IaC) template for your pipeline. Ingestion and updating your application’s Retrieve calls stay with you, and your agent can walk you through both. In this post, we explain why we recommend the move and how the migration guide works, review the prerequisites, install the skill, plan a migration, update the application’s retrieval call, and validate retrieval before cutover. Why move to Managed Knowledge Base We recommend Managed Knowledge Base because it balances ease of use, retrieval accuracy, and cost. AWS runs the store With a Managed Knowledge Base, Amazon Bedrock handles ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval, and the store scales automatically as your content grows. Hybrid search, which combines keyword and semantic matching, is always on, with no index to configure. The knowledge base includes a managed embedding model, a managed reranker, and a built-in parser for multimodal file types. You can still bring your own Amazon Bedrock embedding model when you create the knowledge base. On each retrieval request, you choose the managed reranker, an Amazon Bedrock reranking model, or no reranking. The managed reranker requires the managed embedding model. Built-in capabilities Managed Knowledge Base includes capabilities you’d otherwise build yourself: Native connectors ingest content directly from sources such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence. For the current list, see supported connectors . After the first full sync, later syncs pick up only changes, on demand or on a schedule. The Managed Knowledge Base includes a deletion safeguard to help protect against accidental bulk removal of indexed content. Access control list (ACL) awareness ingests document permissions with the content, so retrieval returns only what the signed-in user can access. For connectors that support it, such as Microsoft SharePoint and Atlassian Confluence, a real-time check against the source also catches permission changes since the last sync. ACL awareness doesn’t authenticate users, so your application must verify and pass the user’s identity. Agentic retrieval answers questions that a single search can’t by handling multi-part questions and retrieving iteratively. It can search more than one knowledge base in a single request. Integration with AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes your knowledge base as a target. Any client that supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can then query the knowledge base, and the gateway handles authentication. Resource-based policies let applications in other AWS accounts use one team’s knowledge base. Scope each policy to the specific roles that call the knowledge base, and grant only the actions they use, such as bedrock:Retrieve . Agentic retrieval, AgentCore Gateway integration, and resource-based policies are not available on customer-managed knowledge bases. Fo

title: Build composable, interoperable multi-agent systems with A2A on AWS
abstract: Agents in multi-agent systems that span organizational boundaries often need to collaborate in a composable, interoperable way, with agents that other organizations build and run. They need a way to discover each other, communicate, and exchange tasks without exposing internals or requiring the same framework on both sides. The Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol addresses this constraint. Without A2A, building composable multi-agent systems across organizational boundaries requires custom integration code for each customer and framework. Independent software vendors (ISVs) can instead build composable, interoperable agents that work with the A2A-compatible frameworks their customers already use. While we frame this post around the ISV use case, the pattern also applies to organizations that expose agents across boundaries, whether to partners, customers, or internal teams that use different frameworks. As your system grows, you add skills by registering Agent Cards with the orchestrator, without changing the agents already running. In this post, we walk through a deployed reference architecture on AWS. A LangChain-based enterprise orchestrator communicates with a Strands Agents-based software as a service (SaaS) agent across organizational boundaries using A2A, with the enterprise and the SaaS provider in separate AWS accounts. Neither side depends on the other’s framework or SDK, and the two sides share no secrets. We cover the architecture and implementation patterns, then deploy the system from three Jupyter notebooks and run an end-to-end test. The A2A protocol is now a Linux Foundation project , and AWS is among the organizations that support it. With A2A, agents can discover each other, negotiate tasks, and collaborate across organizational boundaries through a standardized protocol. The protocol uses existing authentication standards such as OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) for cross-boundary security, and is designed to work across A2A-compatible frameworks. In Open Protocols for Agent Interoperability Part 4: Inter-Agent Communication on A2A , we introduced A2A concepts and demonstrated two Strands agents communicating using the protocol on AWS. That post established the foundation with Agent Card discovery, structured task execution, and the A2A server pattern. This post builds on that foundation with cross-framework interoperability, cross-organizational trust boundaries, and OAuth in both directions. Solution overview Three agents run in two AWS accounts, one for the enterprise and one for the SaaS provider. The A2A protocol connects them, with OAuth authentication in both directions. Each account has its own Amazon Cognito user pool, so each side authenticates with its own identity provider. Figure 1: A2A agents across an enterprise account and a SaaS provider account During onboarding, the enterprise and the SaaS provider exchange only public values, such as identity provider URLs, client IDs, scopes, and endpoint URLs. Each side then trusts tokens from the other side’s user pool, and no secrets are shared. After onboarding, each request follows these steps: The enterprise app gets an access token from the enterprise’s Amazon Cognito user pool. The app sends a question over HTTPS to the user API in Amazon API Gateway, then polls for the answer. Amazon API Gateway forwards the request privately, through a VPC link and an internal Network Load Balancer, to the Enterprise Orchestrator, a LangChain agent. When its model decides that the question needs a compliance scan, the orchestrator gets its own token from the enterprise user pool, using a client secret stored in AWS Secrets Manager . The orchestrator sends an A2A request to the compliance SaaS agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, using the skill it read from the agent’s Agent Card at startup. The compliance agent checks the enterprise context agent’s Agent Card at the callback URL registered at onboarding, then gets a token from the SaaS provider’s own pool.

title: Fine-grained access control for Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base tools
abstract: More enterprises are building AI agents into their daily work, and a common pattern is an agent that searches internal documents to compose its answers. A single organization might soon run hundreds of agents, each connected to many data sources and tools. This raises a question. When an agent searches on behalf of a user, can you make sure that it uses only the information that user is allowed to see? Consider AnyCompany, a fictional company that builds an internal assistant shared by all employees. An employee in department A asks, “Compare my department’s business plan with the notice to all departments, and list the initiatives that are behind schedule.” The agent writes its own search queries and keeps searching internal documents until it has enough information. Employees in department B ask the same assistant the same question. If the application doesn’t scope searches to each user, the department B business plan can end up in an answer to an employee in department A. If you replace the departments with customer companies, the same problem occurs in a multi-tenant software as a service (SaaS) architecture where multiple customers share one assistant and knowledge base. Controlling access to multi-tenant data through this agent is harder than in traditional applications. In a traditional application, the application code determines who the signed-in user is and searches with that user’s permissions. In an agent, a large language model (LLM) decides at runtime which tool to call and with which arguments. If a search tool takes “who to search as” as an argument, the LLM decides that value too. A prompt injection or an LLM error might then make the agent search as a different employee. In this post, we build an internal assistant for AnyCompany. All employees share the same agent and knowledge base, yet each employee can search only the documents they’re allowed to view. We use Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base as the search backend and expose it to the agent as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The design principle is to not let the LLM decide who the user is. Instead, trusted code decides, based on information that your identity provider has verified. On top of that, we add independent layers of defense in case that mechanism has a bug or is bypassed. Solution overview Managed Knowledge Base has a feature called ACL awareness . When a search request includes a user context ( userContext ) with the user’s email in userId , the knowledge base returns only the documents that user is allowed to view. If your application calls the search API directly, the application code sets the search scope from the authentication result. Build multi-tenant agentic chat applications on enterprise data with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base shows this pattern. When you expose the knowledge base as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway, however, userContext becomes a tool argument, and the LLM constructs its value. Neither the gateway nor the knowledge base verifies that this value belongs to the authenticated user. This solution injects verified user attributes into tool calls at the tool layer (AgentCore Gateway). It then scopes the search by those attributes at the resource layer (Managed Knowledge Base). The sample stores three documents in a single knowledge base: business plans for department A and department B, and a notice shared with all departments. Two users, user-a in department A and user-b in department B, search through the same agent. The following diagram shows the architecture. title: From prototype to production: Engineering agents with Agent DLC
abstract: Over the past year, AI agents have moved from exploration into engineering. Enterprise teams are shipping large language model (LLM) systems that call tools, orchestrate APIs, and answer questions over internal knowledge. A successful demo can show what an agent is capable of. Before release, the team needs to answer a further question: “ Is this agent ready for production? ” The person responsible for that decision needs evidence that the agent meets the agreed requirements. To make that decision consistently, teams need a repeatable, affordable way to assess the agent’s current behavior and whether the latest change has improved it. In traditional software development, teams answer these questions with unit tests, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD), and passing builds. Those mechanisms are necessary but not sufficient for agents, for three reasons, each requiring additional checks. This post explains these three properties and presents a measured case where an aggregate metric hides a coverage problem. It then introduces the Agent Development Lifecycle (Agent DLC): one lifecycle, two loops, and a single explicit standard for judging every change. A note on terminology: Throughout this post, gold standard means one specific artifact: the bundle of verifiable criteria, their thresholds, and the approved examples they are checked against. Business owners approve this standard as the basis for acceptance decisions. 1. Three properties of agents that require additional engineering practices Conventional software testing and CI/CD still apply to agents, but three properties require additional checks. First, agents are non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different outputs and execution paths. Second, changes to prompts, tool descriptions, retrieval settings, or memory configuration can alter behavior in ways that a text review alone can’t reveal. Third, model endpoints, knowledge bases, and external APIs can change independently of the repository and affect agent behavior. Table 1 summarizes the engineering practices needed to address each property. Table 1. What each property invalidates, and what it requires instead. Property The conventional answer Why it falls short What Agent DLC requires Non-determinism One assertion per case in CI Measures a single sample of a distribution. Passes and fails for reasons unrelated to your change Run each example k times. Judge on pass rate and failure distribution Prompts are source code Review the diff, approve the change Behavior can’t be read off the text of a prompt Every prompt, tool, retrieval, and memory change is versioned with an evaluation attached, and the lineage is kept Dependencies move on their own Pin versions, validate on upgrade Doesn’t fire because nothing in your repository changed Re-run the standard on a schedule and alert on deviations from the baseline 2. We built a reference implementation to exercise the method end to end: an internal policy assistant answering HR policy questions over a document knowledge base. We chose a narrow, well-scoped domain to make the evaluation and diagnosis straightforward to follow. The following results were measured on this reference implementation. It isn’t a customer outcome and it isn’t a benchmark result. The accompanying AWS Samples repository includes infrastructure deployment, the HR agent, custom evaluators, and scripts for baseline evaluation and prompt-change re-evaluation ( 09-run-eval.sh and 10-optimize-prompt.sh ). It also includes optional checks for judge repeatability, model comparison, cost, and latency. The scripts reproduce the workflow. Scores can vary across runs and repository versions. title: Build autonomous AI agents with Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI
abstract: Java teams have established JVM tooling, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines, and operational patterns, yet taking AI agents from prototype to production is hard: agent frameworks do not solve scalability, governance, security, and operational concerns by default. Amazon Bedrock and Spring AI close those gaps, so Java teams can build autonomous AI agents that plan, call tools and APIs, and maintain context across multi-turn conversations. Agentic AI is moving beyond prompt-response interactions toward autonomous systems that execute complex multi-step tasks. Java remains one of the widely used programming languages in enterprise software. Teams have existing CI/CD pipelines, operational expertise, and established patterns built around the JVM. Spring AI brings AI capabilities to the JVM through familiar Spring patterns: auto-configuration, dependency injection, and composable advisors. Developers can build AI agents using the same idioms they use for REST APIs, security, and data access. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. With AgentCore, you can build, deploy, and operate AI agents at scale. It is framework-agnostic and model-agnostic: you bring your preferred agent framework and foundation model (FM). With AgentCore, you can access the production infrastructure you need: managed runtime, memory, browser automation, code execution, and identity management. In this post, we show you how to build autonomous AI agents in Java using Spring AI and Amazon Bedrock with spring-ai-agentcore . We explore the key implementation patterns for two systems. The first is a single-agent travel assistant that demonstrates tool calling and memory. The second is a multi-agent intelligent document processing (IDP) system that shows how specialist agents, a rules engine, and alerting work together. Prerequisites To follow along with this walkthrough, you need the following: Java – JDK 21 (required) Spring Boot – 4.1 (with Spring AI 2.0 and spring-ai-agentcore 2.0) Maven – 3.9+. Node.js – 18+ (for the React frontend) Terraform – 1.5+. Docker – with Buildx for multi-architecture builds. AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) – v2, configured with credentials. An AWS account . What makes a system an agent A chat completion call can generate text, but it can’t decide what to do next, reach into external systems, or remember what happened yesterday. An agent can, because it unites three capabilities: Planning – Given a goal, the model breaks it into steps, prioritizes them, and revises the plan as new information arrives. Tool use – Beyond generating text, the model can select and invoke external functions such as APIs, databases, and code interpreters to act in the world. Memory – Context carries across turns (short-term) and across sessions (long-term), so each decision builds on what came before. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) application has limited tool use (retrieval) but no planning loop. An agent has all three, operating in a goal-directed loop until the task is complete or it determines it cannot proceed. The following diagram shows these capabilities in an end-to-end agentic pipeline, from request to grounded answer. Figure 1: Agentic reference architecture. A request flows through the runtime, guardrails, classification, a specialist agent, tools, the foundation model, memory, rules, and human review to a grounded answer, with resilience and observability as cross-cutting concerns The pipeline has 11 stages. A client submits a document and question. The request passes through a runtime gateway for authentication and rate limiting, then input guardrails screen for harmful content. A router classifies the document and routes it to a specialist agent, which plans its workflow and calls tools, the Amazon Bedrock foundation model, memory, and a rules engine as needed. Codex still runs on the developer workstation. The main design choice is how its model requests reach Amazon Bedrock and where your organization applies policy and operational controls. This Week in AI: Who Gets to Benefit from AI?
abstract: AI is becoming more capable at handling everyday tasks, but benefiting from that progress depends increasingly on where people live, what language they speak, and how much control they have over the technology. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , we examined developments from OpenAI and Anthropic, the growing push for regional AI models, and the challenges of making AI more accessible and responsible. Frontier AI is moving into everyday services OpenAI introduced LifeVal , a benchmark that measures how well AI handles everyday tasks such as finding childcare, managing household budgets, and accessing government services. Scores rose from 49% for GPT-5.2 to roughly 80% for GPT-5.6 and GPT-6 Astra. This could help researchers assess whether improvements in model capabilities translate into useful assistance with daily responsibilities. OpenAI reported that ChatGPT now handles roughly 20% of Google’s search volume in search-like queries, although the company hasn’t explained its methodology. Its new GPT-6 Cyber model , available to approved security teams, aims to help identify and fix software vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, Anthropic began testing read-only banking connections in Claude , allowing some US subscribers to analyze spending and identify unusual charges. As AI assistants take on tasks traditionally handled by banks, search engines, and specialized software, those industries will have to reconsider how they serve customers and protect their data. Anthropic also published FlashProve , a research prototype that uses cryptographic proofs to verify which model generated a response. Separately, nonprofit research organization METR reported that AI assistance may have roughly doubled the pace of progress on certain model development tasks at Anthropic over the past year. The findings don’t establish recursive self-improvement, but they suggest that AI assistance is already speeding up parts of model development. That makes it increasingly important to understand how AI is shaping that progress and to check the reliability of the outputs these systems produce. Regional AI addresses gaps in access We’ve previously discussed the “tokenizer tax,” which makes some languages more expensive to process because they require more tokens than English. New research from the University of Michigan found another disadvantage. In one test, answering questions in Pashto consumed up to 179 times more energy than answering equivalent questions in English, while accuracy also suffered. The findings show how language can affect both the cost and quality of AI services. Countries are responding by investing in models designed around their own languages and infrastructure. Ibero-American countries agreed to form a regional AI alliance to coordinate model development, data sharing, and computing resources. India introduced three domestic models , including EKA-1, which supports 22 Indian languages and English, and two Dhīr models designed to work offline with documents. Offline capabilities could make these systems especially useful in rural areas with unreliable internet access. Indonesia’s GoTo , the UAE’s Jais 3 , and Uganda’s Sunflower V2 are further examples of projects developing AI for local languages. These efforts could give developers more control over AI for local languages and reduce reliance on proprietary AI services, even when some build on open foundation models from larger labs. They could also make AI more useful in languages that existing models handle poorly. For organizations deploying AI across multiple countries, testing performance and cost in each language may reveal problems that English-language benchmarks miss. title: What Makes an Agent Self-Evolving?
abstract: An agent can get better at its job without a new model. It can learn to find useful information, choose the right tool, or check that a task is finished before reporting success. For that experience to help with the next task, something has to carry over: an updated instruction, a lesson saved in memory, or a change to the software that runs the agent. That is what interests me about a self-evolving agent: It can use experience to change how it handles future tasks. Much of that change happens in the harness , the instructions, context, tools, and software around the model. Research such as Harness-RSI explores how agents can change that harness while continuing to use the same model. Of course, a change can make things worse. A saved memory might be wrong, or a new instruction might fix one problem and create another. I think about self-evolving agents in three parts: evaluation to tell whether a change helped, an improvement process that can do more of the work on its own, and the parts of the harness it is allowed to change. Evaluation: What counts as improvement? Before I ask an agent to improve itself, I want to know what doing a better job would look like. A model’s score on a benchmark tells us how it performed on that test. To evaluate an agent built with that model, we also need to ask whether it used the right information, took the right actions, and met the user’s requirements. In a restaurant-planning exercise I developed for teaching evaluation, an agent is given a group’s needs and information about restaurants. Its job is to suggest a place and a time for dinner. The people and restaurants are fictional, but success is easy to understand: Can everyone eat there, afford it, and make it on time? In one test, the agent recommended a restaurant that met everyone’s needs. My evaluation still marked the answer as wrong because it compared the wording with a sample answer I had written. But my answer was only one possible solution. A different recommendation could work just as well. That feedback could lead a self-improving agent to “fix” a decision that was already good. A more useful evaluation would check whether the recommendation met the group’s requirements. If someone’s budget is $25 and the meal costs $28, the plan fails that check. We can build a custom evaluation around those requirements, checking the price, dietary needs, and timing. Other questions require judgment, such as whether the agent clearly explained a trade-off between price and convenience. A person or another model can help assess those. If we asked the agent to make a booking as well, we would need to check that the reservation actually existed. A message saying, “Your table is booked” would not be enough. Evaluating the system means checking what it did, as well as what it said. Once the agent proposes a change, we can test the updated version against the current one. It should still handle tasks it already did well. We should also try cases that were not used to develop or choose the change. Getting one dinner plan right tells us less than handling new groups with different budgets, dietary needs, and schedules. The evaluation should also explain why an answer failed. “The meal costs more than the guest’s budget” gives the agent something specific to investigate. It still needs to find the cause, but it knows where to start. Autonomous improvement: Who carries the work forward? If an engineer has to spot every failure, suggest every change, and start every test, improvement still depends on that person. Autonomous improvement means giving more of this work to the system. It can review past tasks, look for repeated mistakes, propose a change, and test whether the change helps. For example, a more autonomous dinner planner might notice that it repeatedly recommended restaurants people could not afford, even though their budgets were available. It could try a new instruction: remove restaurants that exceed anyone’s budget before comparing the r

title: Generative AI in the Real World: Memory for Personal AI with Duncan Davidson
abstract: This post was created with the assistance of AI, based on a transcript of the conversation. AI tools have started to remember their users, but each tool remembers a different version of the same person. Duncan Davidson, an independent consultant and longtime software engineer, has been trying to connect those fragments. He joined Ben Lorica to discuss what personal AI could do if people could carry their context between services and decide what each service gets to see. They also talked about how AI coding changed web development during Duncan’s time at Webflow, what new developers may lose as entry-level work changes, and why open source projects need new ways to handle AI-assisted contributions. About the Generative AI in the Real World podcast: In 2023, ChatGPT put AI on everyone’s agenda. In 2026, the challenge will be turning those agendas into reality. In Generative AI in the Real World , Ben Lorica interviews leaders who are building with AI. Learn from their experience to help put AI to work in your enterprise. Check out other episodes of this podcast on the O’Reilly learning platform or follow us on YouTube , Spotify , Apple , or wherever you get your podcasts. Takeaways 06.31 The developer’s job is moving toward outcomes. Duncan compared AI coding to desktop publishing, which removed the physical work of assembling pages but left designers responsible for what the page should look like. At Webflow, he saw people use AI tools to make websites faster than they could with earlier tools. For developers, he said, the question has shifted from how quickly they can type code to “What outcome do you want? What are you trying to do with this code, and how can you make it better?” People still need to judge whether an implementation fits the rest of the system. 10.41 New developers still need a way to become experts. Computer science fundamentals still matter when an agent offers several plausible fixes and a person must choose the one that fits a larger system. Ben asked where future engineers will gain that judgment if AI absorbs entry-level tasks. Duncan compared early career work to an apprenticeship in the arts, where even menial assignments expose newcomers to how the whole operation works. Companies that measure only throughput, he warned, may leave too little room for people to learn. 23.07 AI-assisted changes are straining open source review. Duncan described a library he uses in one of his apps. His fixes, along with performance problems Claude noticed, left his version roughly 25 pull requests ahead of the project’s main branch. The maintainers were using AI too, he said. The difficulty was getting useful changes back to the project without overwhelming its review process. His conclusion was that older open source collaboration practices need a “serious retrofit.” 28.27 Personal memory is fragmented across tools. Duncan first had his coding agents save useful information into a collection of Markdown files. Once commercial agents added memory, he found that “Claude knew me one way and ChatGPT knows me another way.” He could push context back to each tool with instructions and occasional reminders, but that solution demands more tinkering than most people want to do. What he wants is a small set of shared mechanisms that let a person carry context across services. 34.01 Portable memory needs boundaries. A prompt’s context, an agent’s memory of recent interactions, and a person’s longer-term knowledge should be able to travel, but Duncan also wants people to control access by scope. He keeps general notes alongside information about his family and finances. His test for a useful system is whether he can say, “Give Claude access to these scopes of my knowledge, but not everything.” That becomes harder when a personal agent encounters knowledge gained at work. title: Why Git Needs Help: Moving from Files to Systems for Source Control
abstract: The shift to agentic reality When Git was designed in 2005, Linus Torvalds solved a brilliant problem for humans collaborating over terminal windows by trading line-by-line diffs. Fast-forward to 2026: Autonomous coding agents don’t think in flat text files or line breaks. They reason across syntax trees, execution traces, call graphs, and type constraints. In my view, forcing an AI agent to engineer complex distributed systems through string matching is like handing a chief software architect a chisel and a stack of sticky notes. File-centric versus system-centric paradigm shift Dimension Legacy file-centric (Git) Agent-native system graph Representation Flat Unicode text streams Tree-Sitter ASTs & CPG nodes Mutation unit Line-by-line string diffs AST node transformations Context overhead 2,000+ line prompt context fills Sub-50 token targeted node payloads State persistence Ephemeral model prompt windows Execution ledgers & reasoning chains Whenever I see engineers try to lock context-blind models into file-centric version control, I watch the consequences compound quickly. Context windows fill with irrelevant churn, API bills surge, and subtle, multifile structural breakages slip past basic syntax checks. Just as critically, standard Git discards the cognitive history of a change. The moment an agent session completes, its execution logs, compiler feedback, and discarded hypotheses evaporate into thin air. Tactical illustration: renaming a distributed method signature Consider updating a core helper signature across 40 dependent services. A traditional string diff forces the agent to read and mutate thousands of lines of surrounding boilerplate text, burning thousands of context tokens per file: --- a/services/auth.py +++ b/services/auth.py @@ -42,7 +42,7 @@ class AuthManager: def validate_session(self, token: str) -> UserSession: - return fetch_user_by_token(token) + return fetch_user_by_token(token, include_metadata=True) In contrast, an AST mutation node isolates the target function symbol, executing the change precisely without passing unneeded ambient text through the prompt window: { "action": "mutate_node", "target_ast_id": "ast_node_89f2a41b", "symbol": "fetch_user_by_token", "update": { "add_argument": { "name": "include_metadata", "value": true } } } This exact bottleneck hit Anthropic in late 2026. As autonomous agent activity pushed monorepo merges beyond 30,000 per day, conventional Git infrastructure simply buckled under the load. To me, unlocking genuine agentic autonomy requires evolving source control along two complementary tracks: shifting to server-hosted, graph-aware architectures, and treating agent reasoning as a first-class, versioned artifact right alongside the code itself. Why text diffs and ephemeral sessions create silent debt Standard diff tools operate purely on raw Unicode strings. When an agent reorders functions or cleans up formatting, string diffs pollute context windows with noise while remaining blind to structural reality. If you modify a single method signature, Git won’t warn you about the dozen callers broken across separate modules. From my experience, feeding 2,000-line source files into prompts just to update a 5-line helper method degrades model attention, burns compute, and inflates overhead at scale. Text diffs versus AST graph mutations Metric / behavior Text diff (unified patch) AST graph mutation Formatting resilience Breaks on whitespace or line-ending changes Immune to syntax formatting shifts Impact analysis Post hoc CI test failures Sub-second static call-graph resolution Token consumption O(file_size) per prompt iteration O(node_delta) per targeted change Compounding this structural blind spot is what I consider our biggest waste: ephemeral session memory. Whenever an agent finishes a task or compacts its context window, its entire diagnostic history—failed attempts, shell outputs, and compiler warnings—disappears. title: Where Are the “Killer Apps” of AI?
abstract: Most of today’s AI entrepreneurs and social media enthusiasts are young. AI is the first technology revolution they’ve lived through. They don’t remember how unbelievably exciting it was in the late 1970s to get your own computer, instead of struggling to get time on one of the vast machines chugging away in what used to be called “the glass house,” an air-conditioned room where from outside you could watch the nine-track tapes being accessed and the refrigerator-sized disk drives spinning. Input and output was on high-speed teletype printers (no screens) and magnetic tape (and before that on punch cards.) They also mostly don’t remember, as I do, writing assembly-language programs in which you moved data from one computer register to another, specified the arithmetic or logical operations to be performed on it, and then specified where to save the result. They look at today’s AI and marvel at how virtually anyone can now generate code. They don’t realize that that’s also how it felt when you could use an interpreted programming language like BASIC to write your own applications instead of writing them in Assembler. They also don’t remember when Dan Bricklin used BASIC to write the first version of VisiCalc in 1979. He went into business with Bob Frankston, who rewrote it in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II. Dan was able to express the idea in Basic; Bob then wrote a tight, efficient version for widespread distribution. People rushed out to buy computers so they could use VisiCalc, and everyone predicted that the VisiCalc “spreadsheet” would put all the accountants out of work. It was the first program to be referred to as a “killer app.” It wasn’t the democratization of programming itself that was the killer app but what Dan and Bob did with it. In the entrepreneurial explosion that followed, databases, graphics, word processing, and other business applications came out of the glass house and, as Bill Gates put it, “onto every desk and into every home.” Dan Bricklin (right) with Bob Frankston, who rewrote VisiCalc in 6502 Assembly Language for the Apple II Image from https://www.digitec.ch/en/page/visicalc-the-first-killer-app-in-computer-history-16230 We saw the same leap from astonishment to innovation to adoption with the World Wide Web. When O’Reilly demonstrated GNN , the first commercial website, to people at a trade show in 1993, attendees couldn’t believe that clicking on a link could pop up an image or a document from another computer thousands of miles away. They didn’t understand the difference between the software application (the web browser) from the network-connected documents with clickable hyperlinks that it acted as a frame for. They didn’t understand that web pages were a new kind of software written in a simple markup language anyone could understand. It didn’t make sense that the web page was a document that in many ways could look and act like a kind of program. And when people did understand, they thought that might be the end of programming. In 1993, everyone thought that the web browser itself was the killer app, and that Marc Andreessen, the young creator of Mosaic, the most popular web browser, which became Netscape, was going to dethrone Bill Gates as the new king of computing. They didn’t realize that the true killer apps of the web were not the web browser and the web server but applications “up the stack” built using the new programming paradigm the web enabled. Those applications weren’t software as we’d known software before. They were database- and application-backed websites delivering services that were previously impossible. I remember thinking of Amazon as the 2005 equivalent to VisiCalc when a friend told me she had just bought her first computer so she could shop on Amazon. Once again, it wasn’t the new capability itself that was the killer app but what developers did with it. What makes a killer app? title: Measuring AI’s Unintended Consequences
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. AI is great for making teams faster. But is it sustainable? What about maintainability, burnout, and lock-in? This is part 3 of my series on assessing AI’s impact on software development. In part 1 , we looked at why assessing impact is important, and what not to do. In part 2 , we looked at how to measure AI’s impact on delivery speed. In this part, we’re looking at how to measure and model the unintended consequences of using AI. Then we’ll wrap up in part 4 with an examination of business outcomes. Finally, an epilogue puts it all together with notes you can share with your CFO. Does maintainability even matter? I can hear it now: “Who cares about namby-pamby issues like maintainability and burnout? It’s a job. If jobs were supposed to be fun, they wouldn’t be called ‘work!’ Suck it up!” So let me be clear: We care about AI’s unintended consequences because they have real economic impact. If code isn’t maintainable, features take longer to write and bugs take longer to fix, taking time away from more valuable work. If people are burned out, they don’t put forth their full effort, and they eventually quit, taking institutional knowledge with them and leading to time-consuming hiring cycles. If you’re locked in, and AI token costs increase, you could be stuck with a choice between a big bill and cutting back on development. Among the people I’ve talked to, there’s widespread agreement that heavy use of AI produces code that humans have trouble understanding. But there’s disagreement about how much that matters. If AI is doing the maintenance, do we care if a human can understand the code? There are strong opinions on this topic on all sides, but not a lot of actual evidence. What’s clear is that the costs of maintenance and other unintended consequences do matter, but only if there are any costs. This is what we need to measure: Is there an impact? And if there is, is it enough to matter? Unfortunately, unlike the rigorous speed trial we discussed in part 2 , unintended consequences are gradual and fuzzy. Your measurements are going to be noisy and lagging. You’ll have to create models and explore scenarios. Ultimately, your decisions will come down to judgment, informed by your measurements and models but not driven by them. One ring to rule them all There is one idea that, while not perfect, does a good job of capturing the majority of unintended consequences. It’s cost of change . Put simply, cost of change is like a tax on the changes you make to your software. When cost of change is low, complicated changes still take time, but they’re achievable. When cost of change is high, even simple changes can take weeks, and complicated changes seem completely out of reach. Cost of change isn’t easy to measure, but there are several indicators you can use to inform your judgment. Value-add percentage Value-add percentage is the percentage of your software development effort that’s spent on things that bring value to your business, such as new features, versus the percentage of effort that’s spent on non-value-add work, such as fixing bugs, resolving incidents, and manual test and release cycles. Non-value-add work is called “muda.” 1 Some muda is necessary, even valuable, but that doesn’t make it value-add. Imagine a demanding and crotchety customer who always asks, “Why didn’t you just do it right the first time?” If that customer won’t pay for something, it’s muda. That’s why bug fixes are muda: “I’m not paying you to fix a bug that shouldn’t be there in the first place!” And performing releases: “Why don’t you just ship it already! How hard can it be?” Sure, bug fixes can be valuable, and releases are necessary, but they’re still muda. I find it useful to distinguish muda further into discretionary and nondiscretionary muda. title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
abstract: Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.” The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs). Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.” Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control. He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it . The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough . Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.” In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy. The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.” As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however. The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants. Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
abstract: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs . For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. title: Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility
abstract: Representatives from Nvidia told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it would be technically possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review in an interview on Thursday, even while an industry group claimed they were “potentially infeasible.” Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips in order to prevent their smuggling to China. It is one of three chip-security bills under consideration for inclusion in the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, each of which is drawing renewed attention after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy. When the Chip Security Act was introduced, in May 2025, lawmakers said the technology to implement it existed, something Nvidia has not publicly confirmed. In March 2026, the Semiconductor Industry Association, of which Nvidia is a member, explicitly opposed the bill and wrote that its mandates for chip tracking were “new, untested, and potentially infeasible.” But privately, Nvidia representatives working with Foster told the lawmaker that the company could implement them. “They never put anything in writing,” Foster says, but during technical discussions on the possibility of such safeguards, their reaction was “yeah, of course we can do this.” This private acknowledgment to Foster goes further than anything Nvidia has previously made public. Other technology Nvidia has built for its customers suggests that the company can indeed offer accurate tracking of its chips’ locations. In December 2025, for example, it announced a new tool called Fleet Intelligence that would allow customers to monitor how its advanced chips were performing across different data center locations. In doing so, the tool could indicate which country chips were in, Nvidia confirmed to Reuters, but the company would not elaborate on whether this technology could be used to prevent smuggling. Nvidia did not respond to requests for comment or confirmation of Foster’s characterization. In early October, when lawmakers were reportedly increasingly concerned about Nvidia’s role in smuggling, MIT Technology Review asked the company if Fleet Intelligence could be used to prevent the practice. It declined to answer directly, instead sending a statement: “Governments and media have found insignificant diversion of controlled US products—a drop in the bucket compared to the ocean of domestic compute China already has.” The recent fallout at Nvidia involves a number of people and companies alleged to be involved in chip smuggling. Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair, runs Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm now under investigation for smuggling advanced GPUs to China. A US Commerce Department inquiry into the company was reportedly halted after invention by Nvidia. Megaspeed reportedly bought chips from Supermicro, a company that packages Nvidia’s chips onto servers. The Chip Security Act as drafted would require a mechanism to track the locations of chips, either by inspections of facilities, attestations by companies, or ping-based location mechanisms. The ping-based technique, the hardest option to circumvent, would require the GPU to send a signal of its location when it comes online. In September, the Center for Security and Emerging Technology found it would be the most cost-effective option. Foster said he did not ask Nvidia’s representatives why they weren’t voluntarily adopting such chip-tracking tools if they could technically do so. But if the requirements of the bill pass as part of the Senate’s National Defense Authorization Act, the new tracking mechanisms would only tell investigators where the chips are, not offer a way to disconnect them if it’s revealed they have been smuggled. title: What to know about this year’s UN climate talks
abstract: It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey. COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20. This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31. In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked. This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations. Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.” So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage. Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. ) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been quite flat over the past few years.) The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when a glacier collapse caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to helping Nepal recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country). Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal. Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support. One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there. title: The Download: preserving minds and weighing open AI risks
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you. To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to keep the brain going, even beyond death. Their ideas range from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones and uploading our memories to the cloud. title: How Microcredentials Help Engineers Build Trustworthy AI
abstract: Engineering teams are moving at breakneck speed to integrate artificial intelligence, but they are running into a formidable new barrier: compliance issues. Translating high-level AI ethics , governance , and auditing into daily operational workflows has become one of the industry’s toughest challenges. “AI ethics” refers to the principles developers use to govern and operate workflows. “Governance” refers to the rules and procedures an organization establishes for AI workflows and how they interact with organizational data. Auditing is the process of assessing and validating systems to ensure safety, fairness, transparency, and legal compliance. Technology leads and systems engineers are responsible for adhering to a structured set of guidelines for standards and processes usually issued by a governing body such as the European Union , the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology , and the International Organization for Standardization . The regulations aim to mitigate issues such as systemic bias , security vulnerabilities, and transparency risks, but they also highlight a critical skills gap. Most traditional computer science, software, and electrical engineering degree programs were built around technical design and system architecture. They do not yet include training in AI auditing, data tracking, or safety protocols for how AI systems interact with people and other technologies. Expecting mid-career engineers to leave their job to attend a full-time two- or four-year program to learn about the topics is not feasible. Yet treating safety and governance as an afterthought can lead to costly product delays, legal exposure, and broken public trust. Targeted microcredential programs can bridge the knowledge gap by helping engineers build skills in compliance, AI ethics, and governance. The benefits of microcredentials Skills-based microcredentials represent the mastery of expertise gained through a learning program. To earn them, learners must demonstrate the skill through a validation assessment. The microcredentials can be stacked, showing a growing skill set in a defined area and allowing learners to earn several microcredentials in one program. Microcredentials also allow engineers to upskill and master critical competencies, such as bias mitigation, algorithmic transparency, and risk auditing, without interrupting their career. Through rigorous skills-validation assessments, microcredentials give tech leaders verifiable proof that their teams can audit systems effectively before deployment. For engineering organizations, microcredentialing creates an agile upskilling pathway. It connects software engineering and hardware design directly to regulatory frameworks, empowering teams to certify systems for safety and compliance within their development life cycles. Translating standards into microcredentials Bridging technical capability and ethical responsibility requires a trusted foundation. IEEE has long been a pioneer in socio-technical standards , most notably through the IEEE 7000 series for ethics in AI system design, a framework created to address ethical considerations during the development life cycle. The IEEE Credentialing Program translates the organization’s world-class standards into actionable, industry-aligned microcredentials. For more than three decades, IEEE has set the gold standard for technical validation and professional certification. By pairing cutting-edge AI governance standards with targeted microcredential programs, IEEE provides engineers and IT leaders with clear, standardized road maps to build systems that are not just technically advanced but also safe, compliant, and worthy of public trust. To learn more about the credentialing program, explore the offerings or connect with an IEEE expert .

title: When Does It Actually Make Sense to Put AI Into Products?
abstract: Over the past few years, the tech industry has rushed to plug a new microchip into every device on the assumption that if you can add AI, you should. Smart-vision toothbrushes , mood-reading household robots , and a host of physical products are invading consumers’ daily lives, reliant on artificial intelligence to learn, predict, and adjust our behavior. But as anyone who’s struggled to update the firmware in their fridge knows, AI doesn’t improve every product. Some product designers are asking where the line is between genuine innovation and a solution looking for a problem. Savannah Kunovsky leads a team of industrial product designers at Ideo , a design consultancy based in San Francisco focused on helping clients unpack when AI becomes a barrier rather than a breakthrough. Kunovsky spoke with IEEE Spectrum about the pressure to integrate AI in everything, where that integration goes wrong, and what companies can do to determine when an AI integration is—and isn’t—a smart choice. When AI makes products worse How much of the current wave of AI integration into physical products is driven by pressure from investors and shareholders to keep up with industry trends? Savannah Kunovsky : Some of it. Teams come to us feeling pressured to show they’re doing something with AI, sometimes because a CEO has promised the board an “AI story” before the next earnings call, or a competitor has just launched an AI-powered version of their product. In all cases, the first thing we do is step back and ask who the product is for and what they’re trying to do. Once that’s clear, the role AI should play, whether large, small, or invisible, usually becomes obvious. There is an appetite for this kind of grounding in the industry right now. People want to cut through the hype and see what works in practice. How do you distinguish between a genuinely helpful AI feature and a gimmick? Kunovsky : The test for an AI gimmick is the same test we’d apply to any product experience: Does it help someone do what they’re trying to do? Answering that means understanding how people would use the product in the real context they’ll be using it. Many companies look straight to large language models (LLMs) because that’s top of their mind, but there is a whole AI toolbox to draw from: computer vision, sensor fusion, on-device models, et cetera. Picking the right capability for the task matters as much as deciding whether to use AI in the first place. As a new interaction paradigm, AI is asking people to change their behavior, so it needs to be simple. When IDEO’s predecessor firm worked on Apple’s first mouse in the early 1980s , the team gave it only one button because people were learning a completely unfamiliar system and the interaction mechanism needed to be effortless. The wearable Humane AI pin used projection instead of a screen-based display, making a dramatic shift from the smartphone interface users already know. Angel Garcia/Bloomberg/Getty Images In which products has AI made the user experience worse? Kunovsky : The clearest examples are products where AI replaced something that already worked. I have a lot of respect for Humane’s AI Pin as a provocation, but the technology [a screenless, wearable smartphone alternative that uses an AI assistant instead of apps] wasn’t ready . The Pin asked people to give up an interface they knew well for one that was slower and less reliable, which is a hard trade-off to ask of anyone. You see versions of this problem everywhere—a voice assistant that mishears a simple command and turns off the wrong light, a customer service bot that keeps you in a loop when you just want a person. In cars, climate and volume controls moved onto touchscreens and voice menus, so something you used to do by feel now takes your eyes off the road. title: NSF’s X-Labs Program Draws Support From Charities and Investors
abstract: When the U.S. National Science Foundation began its X-Labs program in May, the agency said the higher-risk, higher-funded awards would create new kinds of partnerships that would confront urgent scientific and technological challenges. Now the NSF is doubling down on the idea, with an announcement in October that charities, companies, and investment funds would provide X-Lab winners practical support such as laboratory space, software, shared equipment, and access to key data and expert guidance. The help provided by these organizations, which the NSF is calling “ consortium partners ,” will not give them ownership stakes in the X-Labs projects. The addition of the consortium partners may help the initial winners—who will be announced later in November or December and receive US $1.5 million for a 9-month planning phase—reach the aggressive targets needed to compete for much larger $50 million multiyear grants. “It’s a way of telling X-Labs applicants you don’t need to reinvent the wheel, so you’re not spending half of your X-Labs money to go build or buy basic infrastructure,” says Matt Cimaglia , an investor in consortium partners Occam Foundry and Florida Quantum Center . NSF X-Labs Focus on AI, Computing, and More The NSF initially announced two focus areas for the X-Labs program: scientific instruments for sensing and imaging and photonic microchips for quantum systems . In September, the agency followed up with three additional areas in AI for physical devices , decoding biological sequences , and pushing the physical limits of computing . The NSF requires potential X-Labs award recipients to eventually demonstrate autonomy : Leaders for projects must be focused on the work full-time, for example, and must be able to make hiring and spending decisions independently from any university or commercial owners. That agility sets X-Labs apart, along with the risk appetite. Consortium partners saw the potential to provide infrastructure and operations support to allow X-Labs recipients to focus on research. “[We’re] very interested in the enabling structures of R&D,” says Joshua M. Greenberg , program director at the Sloan Foundation, one of the participating partners. Greenberg says that the foundation has supported multiple focused research organizations, or FROs, already. FROs are independent entities in the same vein as what the X-Labs program hopes to create. Unlike university laboratories or larger tech companies, FROs are founded with a time-limited purpose of advancing research in a well-defined area. Because they start with a clean slate, FROs may lack the infrastructure that university or corporate research groups might inherit. To address that lack of infrastructure, bioengineering service firm Ginkgo Bioworks , in Boston, is offering X-Lab winners up to $5 million worth of access to its “cloud lab,” says Jason Kelly , the firm’s CEO and founder. Ginkgo’s cloud lab can conduct complex and flexible laboratory work, and the company will also offer laboratory space and internal datasets that could be useful for training AI models. Kelly is enthusiastic about the potential for X-Labs, which he says have the potential to “pull platforms into existence” like the federal Human Genome Project once did, which enabled a lot of subsequent innovation. As scientific and technology companies become more powerful, Kelly says, it’s natural that governments should revisit how to involve them in government-led science. “The scale of companies is not like it was in the Vannevar Bush era [in the 1940s],” he says, “so how should the United States leverage those [much larger, more capable] companies? It’s silly to leave them on the sidelines.” In 1945, Vannevar Bush wrote an influential report that helped shape the modern NSF and U.S. federal science funding. title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
abstract: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. title: FAA orders third nationwide ground stop in its history
abstract: On Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool , the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy announced the ground stop on X , citing a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers." Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff were troubleshooting the problem. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. "This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights," Mullin said . "There's no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us." Mullin said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis. Read full article Comments

title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
abstract: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same. Read full article Comments

title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
abstract: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
abstract: Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time. Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured. Accidental savanna Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country's four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).
